title: What Defiles: Tradition, the Heart, and a Gentile Mother
summary: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem object that Jesus' disciples eat without ritually washing their hands. Jesus answers that they have set aside God's command for human tradition, using the vow called Corban as his example, and teaches that defilement comes from the heart, not from food. He then crosses into Gentile territory, where a Syrophoenician mother's persistent answer wins healing for her daughter, and in the Decapolis he opens the ears and loosens the tongue of a deaf man.
story:
The feeding of the five thousand and the walk on the sea in chapter 6 showed Jesus as Israel's shepherd, yet Mark ended that chapter by saying the disciples had not understood about the loaves because their hearts were hardened (6:52). Chapter 7 turns the question from who Jesus is to who belongs at God's table and on what terms. A delegation from Jerusalem, the seat of religious authority, raises a question of purity, and Jesus answers in a way that redraws the line between clean and unclean. Then, as if acting out the teaching, he goes into Gentile regions and brings the kingdom's blessings to people many Jews regarded as unclean: a Greek-speaking mother near Tyre and a deaf man in the Decapolis.

The chapter sits in the middle of what readers call the bread section of Mark (6:30 to 8:21), where the word bread keeps returning: the bread the disciples eat with unwashed hands (7:2, 5), the children's bread the woman asks for (7:27), and then the second feeding in Gentile territory in chapter 8. It also looks ahead. The healing of the deaf man, told with spittle, touch, and a private setting, has a twin in the blind man of Bethsaida (8:22-26), and together they frame the disciples' own deafness and blindness (8:18). Beyond Mark, the chapter anticipates the church's hardest early argument, told in Acts 10 and 15 and Galatians 2, over whether Gentile believers must keep the food laws and whether Jewish believers may eat with them.
historical:
The Pharisees were a lay movement within Judaism, devoted to careful observance of the law of Moses and to a body of teaching they called the tradition of the elders. Josephus says they had passed on to the people regulations handed down from the fathers that were not written in the laws of Moses, and that the Sadducees rejected these (Antiquities 13.297; compare 18.12-15 and Jewish War 2.162-166). Paul, a former Pharisee, calls the same body of teaching ‘the traditions of my fathers’ (Galatians 1:14). Scribes were trained experts in the law, and those who came from Jerusalem (verse 1, as in 3:22) carried the weight of the capital into Galilee, as if an official inquiry had arrived.

Much of this oral tradition was later written down in the Mishnah, the collection of rabbinic rulings compiled under Rabbi Judah the Prince around AD 200. It includes a whole tractate on the washing of hands, Yadayim (‘Hands’), and records that hands were washed before eating ordinary food as well as tithe and priestly portions (m. Hagigah 2:5). It also preserves a dispute between the houses of Shammai and Hillel, schools active before AD 70, over whether one washes the hands before or after mixing the cup at a meal (m. Berakhot 8:2), which shows that handwashing before meals was already being practiced and debated in the generation of Jesus. The Torah itself required washing of hands and feet only of priests before they served at the altar (Exodus 30:17-21). Yair Furstenberg (New Testament Studies 54, 2008) has argued that washing hands for common food was a recent Pharisaic development, based on a new idea that impurity passing from hands into food could defile the body from within, and that Jesus' saying in verse 15 answers exactly that idea. Mark explains the practice at length (verses 3 and 4), which is one of the strongest reasons for thinking he wrote for Gentile readers, and his ‘all the Jews’ is a generalization; how widely ordinary Jews outside Pharisaic circles kept these washings is debated.

The vow in verses 11 and 12 is well attested. The Mishnah's tractate Nedarim (‘Vows’) deals with formulas that dedicated property to God or forbade someone to benefit from it, and it tells of a man in Beth Horon whose father was barred by vow from benefiting from him (m. Nedarim 5:6). The same tractate records that the sages came to allow such a vow to be opened when it dishonored a person's parents (m. Nedarim 9:1), so later rabbinic law moved toward Jesus' position. Josephus explains korban to Greek readers as meaning a gift (Antiquities 4.73; Against Apion 1.167), and an ossuary lid from Jebel Hallet et-Turi near Jerusalem, published by Joseph Fitzmyer in 1959, carries an Aramaic inscription declaring its contents qorban, the same formula in stone.

Tyre and Sidon were the old Phoenician port cities on the coast north of Galilee, prosperous from trade and the purple dye extracted from murex shells. Tyre's territory reached inland to the edge of upper Galilee, so the region of Tyre (verse 24) began only a short walk from Jewish villages. The relationship was close and uneasy. The coastal cities depended on the grain of the Galilean countryside (Acts 12:20 shows Tyre and Sidon needing food from Herod Agrippa's land), and Tyre's silver shekel was so reliable that it became the coin of the temple tax, and the Mishnah reckons the silver payments of the Torah by the Tyrian standard (m. Bekhorot 8:7). Yet Josephus singles out the Tyrians as among the people most hostile to the Jews (Against Apion 1.70), and he records that at the outbreak of the war with Rome in AD 66 the Tyrians killed or imprisoned many of the Jews living among them (Jewish War 2.478). Gerd Theissen (Lokalkolorit und Zeitgeschichte in den Evangelien, 1989; in English The Gospels in Context, 1991) argued that the story of the Syrophoenician woman makes best sense against this background: the wealthy Greek-speaking city took the bread of the Jewish countryside, and Jesus' saying about the children's bread would have sounded to a Galilean ear like a reversal of that economic order.

The Decapolis (Greek for ten cities) was a group of Greek cities, most of them east of the Jordan, with Gentile populations and pagan temples. Pliny the Elder lists ten of them in the first century (Natural History 5.74): Damascus, Philadelphia (modern Amman), Raphana, Scythopolis (the only one west of the Jordan), Gadara, Hippos, Dion, Pella, Gerasa, and Canatha. The man delivered from Legion had already proclaimed in the Decapolis what Jesus had done for him (5:20), which may explain why people there bring the deaf man to Jesus. The route in verse 31, north from Tyre to Sidon and then around to the Sea of Galilee and the Decapolis, is roundabout, a trip of many days through mostly Gentile country. Some critics take it as a sign that Mark did not know the geography; others read it as a deliberate extended withdrawal, in keeping with Jesus' wish in verse 24 not to be found.
cultural:
Handwashing before meals in this setting was about ritual purity, not hygiene. The law of Moses treated impurity as a condition, contracted through contact with a corpse, certain skin diseases, bodily discharges, and some animals, that barred a person from the sanctuary until it was removed by time, washing, and sometimes sacrifice (Leviticus 11 to 15; Numbers 19). Impurity was not sin, and becoming impure was often unavoidable and even required, as in burying the dead. The Pharisees sought to extend the purity expected of priests eating holy food to ordinary meals at home, so that the whole people might live as a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6). The marketplace (verse 4) was a place of uncertain contacts, and returning from it called for washing. The list of washed objects (cups, pitchers, bronze vessels, and, in many manuscripts, dining couches) matches the concerns of the Mishnah's tractate Kelim (‘Vessels’). The Greek verb for washing in verse 4 is a form of baptizō, and the noun is baptismos, the ordinary words for dipping and ritual washing before they became Christian terms. The obscure phrase in verse 3, literally ‘with a fist’ (pygmē), is rendered ‘ceremonially’ by the BSB; interpreters have taken it to mean with a cupped handful of water, up to the wrist, or simply thoroughly, and some manuscripts replace it with a word for often. None of this was careless religion; it was a serious attempt to carry God's holiness into daily life, and Jesus' quarrel is not with seriousness but with the order of priorities.

The duty to parents was grave. The fifth commandment, “Honor your father and mother” (Exodus 20:12), was understood in Jewish teaching to include feeding, clothing, and caring for parents in old age, and the law's sanction for cursing a parent was death (Exodus 21:17, quoted in verse 10). Korban (Hebrew qorban) was the word for an offering brought near to God. A person could declare property korban, dedicating it by vow, and the declaration could bar others, including his parents, from benefiting from it, while the owner might go on using it himself until it was actually delivered. Vows were taken with great seriousness because of texts like Numbers 30:2, which says a man who makes a vow must not break his word. Jesus treats this as a way of using a religious act to escape a moral duty, and he adds that it is one of many such cases (verse 13).

The woman in verse 26 is called Hellēnis, a Greek, which in Jewish usage meant a Gentile and here probably also marks her as belonging to the Greek-speaking, more prosperous class of the city; and Syrophoenician by birth, that is, a Phoenician from the province of Syria, as distinct from the Libyan Phoenicians of North Africa. Matthew calls her a Canaanite (Matthew 15:22), the old biblical name for Israel's ancient enemies. Dogs in the Bible are mostly scavengers of the street, unclean and despised (1 Kings 21:23; Psalm 22:16), and dog could be a term of abuse (1 Samuel 17:43; later, Philippians 3:2 and Revelation 22:15). Jesus uses the diminutive kynarion, and the woman takes up the picture of dogs under a family table, as household animals. Whether the diminutive softens the word is debated: many grammarians note that diminutives in the Greek of the period had often lost their force, while N. Clayton Croy (New Testament Studies, 2024) has argued from a study of its uses that kynarion keeps a real sense of small or household dog. Either way the image is sharp, and the woman's answer turns it inside out. Children and dogs in the saying are figures, not labels for persons: the children are Israel, whom God called his son (Exodus 4:22), and the table is God's provision for his people.

The healing of the deaf man uses gestures familiar in the ancient world. Saliva was widely thought to have healing power: Pliny the Elder recommends the spittle of a fasting person for eye disease and other ailments (Natural History 28.7), and Tacitus (Histories 4.81) and Suetonius (Vespasian 7) tell how the emperor Vespasian, at Alexandria around AD 69, was asked to heal a blind man with his spittle. Healers of the time also used private settings, sighs, and foreign words. Mark keeps all these details, but he gives the power to Jesus' look toward heaven and his word, not to a technique. Ephphatha is the Aramaic imperative, ‘be opened’, and Mark translates it, as he does with talitha koum (5:41), korban (7:11), Abba (14:36), and Eloi (15:34); these preserved words let the reader hear Jesus' own language.
literary:
The chapter has two halves. Verses 1 to 23 are a controversy story that widens in three stages, each to a new audience: Jesus answers his critics with Scripture and an example (6 to 13), addresses the crowd with a short riddle-like saying (14 and 15), and explains it privately to the disciples in the house (17 to 23), the same pattern of public saying and private explanation as in the parables of chapter 4 (4:10-20). Mark calls the saying of verse 15 a parable (verse 17), which in his usage means a pointed saying that needs interpretation. His aside in verse 3 and 4 explains Jewish customs for outsiders, and his aside at the end of verse 19, “Thus all foods are clean,” draws out an implication that the early church came to recognize. The Greek participle there, katharizōn, is masculine and most naturally refers back to Jesus as the one speaking in verse 18 (‘he said… making all foods clean’), which is why many versions render it ‘Thus he declared all foods clean’; the BSB puts it in parentheses as the narrator's comment.

The controversy is built as an argument from Scripture. Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13 in a form close to the Greek Old Testament, whose last line (‘teaching as doctrines the precepts of men’) fits his point more sharply than the Hebrew, which the BSB renders “Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men” (Isaiah 29:13). Then he contrasts two sayings: “Moses said” (verse 10) against “you say” (verse 11), commandment of God against tradition of men, repeated three times (verses 8, 9, and 13) with rising sharpness: they ‘disregard’ the command, they ‘neatly set aside’ it, they ‘nullify’ it. The word ‘neatly’ (kalōs, ‘well’) in verse 9 is ironic, the same word Jesus uses for Isaiah prophesying ‘correctly’ in verse 6 and the crowd uses when it says he has done all things ‘well’ in verse 37. The vice list in verses 21 and 22 names ‘evil thoughts’ and then twelve evils, six in the plural (sexual immoralities, thefts, murders, adulteries, greedy acts, wickednesses) and six in the singular (deceit, debauchery, an evil eye, which is a Semitic idiom for envy or stinginess, slander, arrogance, foolishness). Such lists appear in Greek moral writing and in Paul (Romans 1:29-31; Galatians 5:19-21); this one moves from deeds to dispositions and ends with foolishness, the root of the others in the wisdom tradition.

Verses 24 to 37 are two healings in Gentile territory, and each answers the first half. The woman argues with Jesus and wins, the only person in Mark who does, and her word ‘Lord’ (kyrie) is the only time anyone in Mark addresses Jesus by that title. Jesus says her daughter is healed ‘because of this answer’ (literally ‘because of this word’), a healing at a distance, the only one in Mark. The second healing ends with a crowd's verdict that echoes Isaiah 35:5-6, where the ears of the deaf are unstopped and the tongue of the mute shouts for joy. The rare Greek word for the man's speech defect in verse 32, mogilalos, ‘speaking with difficulty’, appears nowhere else in the New Testament and in the Greek Old Testament only in Isaiah 35:6, which strongly suggests Mark wants readers to hear that chapter. The crowd's words, ‘He has done all things well’, may also recall the verdict on creation in Genesis 1:31, though the Greek wording is not the same. Finally, the chapter prepares for chapter 8: the deaf man healed privately with spittle and touch has his twin in the blind man of Bethsaida (8:22-26), and between them stands Jesus' question to his disciples, ‘Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?’ (8:18).

outline.t: God's command and human tradition: Isaiah and Corban
What truly defiles comes from the heart
A deaf and mute man healed in the Decapolis

doctrines.note: Jesus upholds the commandment to honor father and mother against a tradition that evaded it (verses 9 to 13), treating the written law as the word of God by which all tradition is judged. At the same time his saying that nothing entering from outside defiles, with Mark's comment that all foods are clean (verse 19), points to a fulfillment in which the food laws' purpose, a holy people set apart for God, is met in a cleansed heart. Christians differ on how far Jesus himself set aside the food laws and how far the church drew the conclusion later.

Jesus locates the source of evil not in outside contamination but in the human heart (verses 21 to 23). The list of evils shows that sin is first a matter of what people are, not only what touches them, and that no washing can reach it. The same diagnosis runs from Jeremiah 17:9 to Romans 7.

The case Jesus chooses is about the family. The fifth commandment binds children to honor and support their parents, and Jesus treats a religious vow that frees a son from that duty as nullifying the word of God (verses 10 to 13). Care for aging parents is not a lesser, merely domestic duty beneath worship; it is part of the worship God commands, and no gift to God can be paid with what is owed to them.

Jesus' travel into Tyre, Sidon, and the Decapolis anticipates the gospel's spread to the Gentiles. The order he states, children ‘first’ (verse 27), is Paul's order too, “first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16), but the woman's answer shows that the bread was always meant to reach beyond Israel's table.

The Syrophoenician mother never uses the word faith in Mark, but she shows it: she falls at Jesus' feet, keeps asking, accepts the order he names, and trusts that even a crumb from his table is enough. Jesus answers her word with healing at a distance.

words.note: Paradosis, tradition, literally something handed over. It occurs thirteen times in the New Testament, five of them in this chapter (verses 3, 5, 8, 9, 13), and three in Matthew's parallel. The word is not negative in itself: Paul uses it for the apostolic teaching he passed on (1 Corinthians 11:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:15) as well as for his former zeal for his ancestral traditions (Galatians 1:14) and for human traditions opposed to Christ (Colossians 2:8). BDAG describes it as the content of what is handed on. Jesus' charge is not that tradition exists but that this tradition, called ‘the tradition of men’ in verse 8, was allowed to override the command of God.

Koinoō, to make common, that is, ritually impure; used five times in this chapter (verses 15, 18, 20, 23, and, in some manuscripts, 2) and about fourteen times in the New Testament. Its root is koinos, common, which in Jewish Greek meant the opposite of holy or set apart; Peter uses koinos when he protests that he has never eaten anything ‘common or unclean’ (Acts 10:14), and the voice replies with the related verb, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). Jesus turns the category inward: what makes a person common, unfit to stand before a holy God, is what comes out of the heart.

Korban, a Greek spelling of the Hebrew qorban, an offering, from the verb for bringing near. In the Old Testament it is the standard word for sacrifices and gifts brought to God, especially in Leviticus and Numbers. Mark keeps the foreign word and translates it for his readers as ‘a gift devoted to God’. Matthew 27:6 uses the related korbanas for the temple treasury. Here it names a vow that took property off the table for others, used to dodge a clear duty.

Kardia, heart, about 156 times in the New Testament and eleven in Mark, three of them here (verses 6, 19, 21). In biblical usage the heart is not chiefly the seat of feeling but the center of the person, where thought, will, and desire are formed, as in the Hebrew lev. The chapter's argument turns on the word: the people honor God with their lips while their heart is far off (verse 6), food cannot defile because it does not enter the heart (verse 19), and evil comes out of the heart (verse 21). Mark has already said the disciples' hearts were hardened (6:52), and he will say it again (8:17).

Katharizō, to make clean, cleanse, declare clean; about thirty-one times in the New Testament. Mark uses it for the cleansing of the leper (1:40-44) and here for the declaration that all foods are clean (verse 19). The same verb appears in Peter's vision (Acts 10:15; 11:9) and in the promise that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). In verse 19 the participle's gender decides whether Jesus is the one declaring foods clean (the masculine of the earliest manuscripts) or the digestive process is described as purging them (the neuter of the later Byzantine text, followed by the KJV).

Hypokritēs, hypocrite. In classical Greek it meant a stage actor, one who plays a part behind a mask, and then someone who pretends. It occurs about seventeen times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels and most often in Matthew; this is its only use in Mark. Jesus uses it here for people whose religious performance is detached from the heart that Isaiah said God looks for.

Kynarion, little dog or house dog, a diminutive of kyōn, dog. It occurs only four times in the New Testament, in this story and Matthew's parallel (Mark 7:27, 28; Matthew 15:26, 27). Scholars debate whether the diminutive still carried a softening force in the Greek of the period. The woman in any case seizes the picture of a dog inside the house, under the table, and argues from it: household dogs eat from the same meal, even if they eat what falls.

Mogilalos, speaking with difficulty, from mogis, hardly, and laleō, to speak. It occurs only here in the New Testament and only once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 35:6, where it renders the Hebrew for the mute whose tongue will shout for joy when God comes to save. Its rarity makes it one of the clearest verbal signals in Mark that an Old Testament promise is being fulfilled. When the man is healed he speaks orthōs, ‘plainly’ or ‘correctly’ (verse 35).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the one with authority to interpret the law and to declare what makes a person clean. He does not argue as one teacher among others, citing earlier authorities; he sets the command of God against the tradition of men and then pronounces on the purity laws themselves, as Mark's comment in verse 19 draws out. In Israel's Scriptures the one who declares clean and unclean is God, who gave the distinctions (Leviticus 11:44-47), and his priests, who applied them. Jesus speaks with that authority, which is why Mark's readers, many of them Gentiles, heard in his words the ground of their welcome at the church's table.

The second half of the chapter shows him fulfilling Isaiah 35. That chapter promises, “Behold, your God will come” (Isaiah 35:4), and then, “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). Mark's rare word for the man's speech impediment and the crowd's closing cry echo that passage directly, so that the healing is presented as a sign that Israel's God has come to save. The link is not a loose theme but a deliberate verbal echo, and it fits Mark's opening, where the one whose way is prepared is the Lord himself (1:2-3). The same healing shows the manner of his coming: he takes the man aside, touches the very places of his affliction, looks to heaven, and sighs (stenazō), a word Paul uses for the groaning of those who wait for redemption (Romans 8:23). The Savior of this chapter enters bodily into human brokenness.

In the region of Tyre Jesus gives Israel's bread to a Gentile mother. Mark has already shown him delivering a Gentile man in the Decapolis (5:1-20); here the order of salvation is spelled out, the children first, and then overcome by grace for the one who asks. Jesus' mission in the Gospels is first to Israel (Matthew 15:24), and his answer to the woman keeps that order while showing that the promise to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), was never an afterthought. The deeper cleansing the chapter points to, a heart made new, is what the prophets promised (Ezekiel 36:25-27) and what the New Testament says Christ accomplishes by his death and the gift of the Spirit, so that Peter can later say God cleansed the Gentiles' hearts by faith (Acts 15:9).
interpretation:
Jewish readers have long recognized the debate of verses 1 to 13 as an argument within Judaism. The Mishnah's rulings on handwashing (Yadayim) and on releasing vows made against parents (m. Nedarim 9:1) show the same questions under discussion among the sages. A famous later saying attributed to Yohanan ben Zakkai, the first-century sage who refounded Jewish learning at Yavneh after AD 70, makes a point that sounds close to Jesus' and then turns the other way: after explaining the red heifer ritual to a Gentile, he told his students that a corpse does not in itself defile nor the water purify, but that the ritual is a decree of the Holy One, which Israel may not transgress (Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 4:7). For the rabbis the inner meaning of purity did not cancel its practice. Modern Jewish scholars have read Mark 7 closely in that light. Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012, in a chapter titled ‘Jesus Kept Kosher’) argues that Mark's Jesus defends the written Torah against the Pharisees' newer rules and that ‘all foods’ means all permitted foods, eaten without handwashing; the Christian scholar James Crossley (The Date of Mark's Gospel, 2004) made a similar argument and used it to date Mark as early as the late 30s or early 40s. Most commentators, including Joel Marcus and R. T. France, hold that Mark's comment in verse 19 does draw the conclusion that the food laws no longer bind, whatever Jesus' first hearers understood.

The church fathers read the chapter through Matthew's fuller parallel. Origen, in his Commentary on Matthew (book 11, written in the 240s), discussed the Corban vow and the relation of the law to the traditions of the elders at length. Hilary of Poitiers (Commentary on Matthew, around 355) and many after him read the Canaanite or Syrophoenician woman as a figure of the Gentile church, begging for her daughter, the Gentile peoples held by unclean spirits. The Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, a romance compiled from earlier sources by the fourth century, gave her a name, Justa, and her daughter the name Bernice, and made her a convert who gave up Gentile food practices (Homilies 2.19), a telling sign that some Jewish-Christian circles read the story as a warrant for Gentiles keeping the food laws. Augustine and Chrysostom praised her humility and persistence as a model of prayer, and that reading became the church's standard.

The healing of the deaf man entered the church's baptismal rites. Ambrose of Milan (On the Sacraments 1.2-3, around 390) describes the bishop touching the ears and nostrils of candidates before baptism and saying Ephphatha, the ‘opening’, so that they might hear the word and receive the fragrance of faith. The rite passed into the Roman ritual, and the reformed Catholic rite of baptism after the Second Vatican Council keeps an optional Ephphatha prayer over the ears and mouth. The Reformers used verses 6 to 13 in their arguments over human traditions in worship: Calvin's Harmony of the Gospels (1555) and the Lutheran confessions both appeal to the charge that God is worshiped in vain by the precepts of men, while Catholic writers answered that apostolic tradition, which Paul himself commends (2 Thessalonians 2:15), is not what Jesus condemns here. Verse 19 divided translators: the King James Version, following the Byzantine neuter participle, reads that the draught ‘purgeth all meats’, while the Revised Version of 1881 and nearly all modern versions follow the masculine and make the clause a statement that all foods are clean.

Modern scholarship has debated the Syrophoenician story more than any other part of the chapter. T. A. Burkill (Novum Testamentum, 1967) traced how the saying about children and dogs developed as the early church argued over the Gentile mission. Gerd Theissen (1989) read it against the economic tensions between Tyre and the Galilean countryside. Feminist interpreters, beginning with Sharon Ringe's essay ‘A Gentile Woman's Story’ in Feminist Interpretation of the Bible (edited by Letty Russell, 1985), read the woman as the one who teaches Jesus and widens his mission, and postcolonial readers have taken up her place on the border between peoples. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Mark 7:1-8, 14-15, 21-23 is read in Year B on Proper 17 and Mark 7:24-37 on Proper 18, paired with Isaiah 35:4-7a; the Roman lectionary reads the same passage on the Twenty-Second Sunday in Ordinary Time and the healing of the deaf man (7:31-37) on the Twenty-Third. In art the woman at Jesus' feet was painted by Jean-Germain Drouais, a pupil of Jacques-Louis David, whose The Woman of Canaan at the Feet of Christ won the Prix de Rome in 1784 and now hangs in the Louvre.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts.

Verse 4: the words ‘and couches for dining’ are missing from several of the oldest manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and present in Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae, Codex Washingtonianus, and most later ones. The Nestle-Aland and SBL editions print them; Westcott and Hort omitted them. The BSB includes them; the ESV and NIV note the question.

Verse 16: ‘If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear’ is absent from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and other early witnesses, and critical editions omit it; it appears in most later manuscripts and in the King James Version, and probably entered from 4:9 and 4:23. The BSB leaves the verse number empty.

Verse 19: the oldest manuscripts, among them Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Alexandrinus, read the masculine participle katharizōn, which makes the clause a comment about Jesus: he declared all foods clean. The Byzantine text read by the Textus Receptus has the neuter katharizon, which attaches the clause to the process of digestion, and the King James Version renders it ‘purging all meats’. The difference is one letter, but it changes the sentence from anatomy to theology, and almost all modern versions follow the older reading.

Verse 24: many manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘the region of Tyre and Sidon’. The shorter reading ‘Tyre’ is found in early witnesses of several kinds (Bezae, Washingtonianus, Koridethi, and others), and most editors think ‘and Sidon’ was added from Matthew 15:21 and Mark 7:31. Verse 31: where modern editions read that Jesus went ‘through Sidon’ to the Sea of Galilee, the Byzantine text, followed by the KJV, reads that he departed ‘from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon’ and came to the sea, which smooths the unusual route.

Verses 6 and 7 quote Isaiah 29:13 in a form close to the Greek Old Testament, whose wording, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men, differs from the Hebrew, which speaks of fear of God as a commandment of men learned by rote. The New Testament follows the Greek, and the point is the same in both: worship that is only human instruction.

teach.big: What makes a person unfit for God is not what touches us from outside but what comes out of our own hearts, and the Jesus who exposes the heart is the same Jesus who crosses every boundary to heal and feed those who ask.

outline.t: Religious seriousness can harden into a system that watches other people's hands and forgets its own heart.
God's word judges every tradition, and a tradition that lets us look devout while neglecting the people God gave us to care for has turned worship into performance.
Defilement starts inside: the heart, not the menu or the marketplace, is where evil is born, and only a cleansing that reaches the heart can make us clean.
Faith takes Jesus at his word, accepts the order of God's grace, and still asks boldly, trusting that even a crumb from his table is enough.
When God comes to save, the deaf hear and the mute speak; Jesus fulfills that promise with a personal, bodily, praying compassion.

teach.pitfalls:
The first misreading turns the Pharisees into cartoons of legalism. Their purity practice was a serious attempt to make all of life holy, and many of their own teachers agreed with Jesus about vows against parents. Preaching that sneers at them misses the point, which is that devout people of every age, including churchgoers, can let their traditions override God's command. The second pitfall is to conclude that tradition as such is bad. Jesus judges traditions by the word of God; he does not reject the church's handing on of the faith, which Paul commends (1 Corinthians 11:2).

A third error reads verses 14 to 23 as permission to treat outward things as unimportant, as if the body, food, and behavior did not matter so long as the heart is right. Jesus' list is a list of deeds (theft, murder, adultery) that come from the heart, not a license to ignore them. A fourth takes the saying that nothing from outside defiles as a denial that outside influences can harm anyone. Jesus is speaking of ritual defilement before God, not denying that what we watch, hear, and consume can shape desire (compare 9:42-47). The fifth concerns the Syrophoenician woman. Some preaching makes Jesus' reply a simple test with a wink, and some makes it proof that Jesus was a bigot corrected by a woman; the text supports neither easy version. It is better to let the saying's sharpness stand, note the word ‘first’, and follow Mark in praising the woman's answer. Finally, avoid making the spittle and fingers of verse 33 into a technique for healing; Mark shows that the power lies in Jesus' prayer and word.
teach.pastoral: The chapter can press hard on people raised in religious systems that measured holiness by outward conformity, and on those who carry shame from being treated as unclean because of their background, ethnicity, or past. Teach verses 14 to 23 as release from a false standard, not as a new burden of introspection; people prone to scrupulosity may hear the vice list as an accusation they can never escape. Pair it with Mark's picture of Jesus touching the deaf man and answering the Gentile mother. The Corban example touches families strained by the care of aging parents, and some in the room will feel guilt for not doing more while others carry resentment at duties they cannot sustain; the text condemns evasion by religious excuse, not the hard limits of real caregivers. Parents of sick or troubled children will hear the Syrophoenician mother's persistence with special force, and they should hear too that Jesus answered her.

hard.q: Why does Jesus seem to insult the Syrophoenician woman by comparing her to a dog?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. Jesus refuses a desperate mother's plea for her daughter and justifies it with a saying that likens her people to dogs, a word used in the Bible and later Jewish writing for the despised and unclean. Sharon Ringe (1985) called the reply flippant and even cruel, beyond justification, and argued that the woman corrects Jesus and widens his mission. Many feminist and postcolonial interpreters have followed that line, and skeptical readers take the saying as evidence that the historical Jesus shared the ethnic prejudices of his time, which the church later softened. Jewish readers have sometimes noted, with some justice, that Christian commentators who explain the saying away often do so by portraying Judaism as the source of the contempt, when the saying is on Jesus' own lips. Matthew's version sharpens the difficulty, adding Jesus' silence and the words “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

Responses take several forms. Some stress the saying's form: the word ‘first’ in verse 27 implies that Gentiles will be fed after Israel, so the saying states an order of mission, not an exclusion, and N. Clayton Croy (New Testament Studies, 2024) argues that the diminutive kynarion means household dogs rather than street curs. Many interpreters from Chrysostom onward read the saying as a test or a riddle-like challenge that invites the woman's reply, in the way a teacher sets a problem; she treats it that way, and Jesus praises her ‘word’. Others read it as Jesus voicing the common view in front of his disciples in order to overturn it, immediately after teaching that food cannot make anyone unclean. Those who hold, with Ringe, that Jesus learned from her, draw on the church's confession of his full humanity; others answer that nothing in Mark shows Jesus changing his mind, only granting what she asks on the ground of her answer. The order of Israel first is a second-order question on which Christians hold different emphases. What is not in dispute is the outcome: a Gentile woman, persistent and humble, receives exactly what she asked, and Mark presents her as a model of faith at a moment when the disciples are still dull of understanding.

hard.q: Did Jesus abolish the Jewish food laws, and if so, why did the early church argue about them?
hard.a:
The objection has two forms. Jewish scholars such as Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012), with Christian scholars such as James Crossley (2004), argue that the historical Jesus, and even Mark's Jesus, never set aside the Torah's food laws: the dispute in verses 1 to 5 concerns handwashing, a Pharisaic tradition, not the biblical laws of Leviticus 11, and ‘all foods’ means all foods the Torah permits. On this view the traditional reading makes Jesus reject his own Scriptures, which his first followers plainly did not believe. Skeptical readers press the same point from another side: if Jesus had declared all foods clean, why did Peter need a vision to eat with Gentiles (Acts 10:9-16), why did he withdraw from Gentile tables at Antioch (Galatians 2:11-14), and why does Matthew, retelling this scene, omit Mark's comment?

Responses begin with the text. Most commentators (among them Joel Marcus and R. T. France) note that the parenthesis in verse 19 is Mark's own comment, drawing out what the saying of verse 15 implies for a church of Jews and Gentiles; they do not claim that the disciples grasped it at the time, and Mark says they did not (verse 18). Jesus' argument is about what defiles a person before God, and a principle stated about the heart can take years to be worked out at the table, as Acts shows. Others argue that Jesus relativized purity without abolishing it, teaching that moral defilement matters more than ritual, in line with the prophets (Hosea 6:6), and that the church later drew the full conclusion under the Spirit's guidance (Acts 15:28-29; Romans 14:14). Matthew's omission is usually explained by his Jewish-Christian audience and his emphasis that Jesus came to fulfill the law (Matthew 5:17). Christians have held these readings side by side, and the question of how Jesus' own practice related to Mark's comment remains open among interpreters of every tradition.

observe: List the words Jesus uses in verses 8, 9, and 13 for what the Pharisees do with God's command. How does the charge grow sharper?
What details does Mark give about how Jesus heals the deaf man (verses 33 and 34), and which of them are unusual?
What exactly does the woman say in verse 28, and how does it take up the words Jesus used in verse 27?
interpret: Why does Jesus answer a question about handwashing with a case about vows and parents? What connects the two?
What does Mark mean by adding ‘Thus all foods are clean’, and why would that matter to a church of Jews and Gentiles?
How does Isaiah 35 help explain why the crowd says ‘He has done all things well’?
apply: What traditions in your church or family might, like Corban, allow people to look devout while avoiding a clear duty to someone close to them?
Jesus says evil comes from within. How does that change the way you think about protecting yourself or your children from outside influences, without dismissing them?
The Syrophoenician woman accepted a hard word and still pressed her request. What does her way of praying teach you about persistence and humility before God?
